• Other names: Blyxa, Bamboo plant, Roundfruit blyxa
  • Minimum tank: 80 litres (20 gallons)
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Hardness: soft
  • Growth form: rosette; growth rate moderate
  • Placement: background
  • CO2 and fertilizer needed
  • Propagation: vegetative and by seeds

In Malaysia, Blyxa aubertii is eaten raw as a vegetable. It is also used as a raw material for papermaking.

Blyxa aubertii is native to tropical and subtropical regions of Asia, northern Australia, and West and Central Africa.

It occurs in India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Vietnam, China, Taiwan, Korea and Japan (Ryukyu Islands), as well as Africa and Australia.

The species was brought to North America approximately 40 years ago. It was first found in Louisiana and has now also been recorded in Mississippi.

Although it occurs in many places, it almost never dominates over other plant species.

Blyxa aubertii grows in wetlands and lowlands. It is usually found in slow, very shallow water in encroached mangrove land, paddy fields and canals.

It is an annual aquatic plant with leaves forming a rosette on a short, erect rhizome. It can grow up to 50 cm tall and about 25 cm wide. The natural colour is light green, but under intense light it takes on deep reddish/purple shades. The leaf blade is sessile, linear with an elongated tapering tip, up to 50 cm long and 0.5–1 cm wide; the leaves are soft, thin and brittle.

The flowers are bisexual (self-pollinating) and solitary, with white or reddish petals. Flowers and fruits can be produced both below and above the water surface. In aquariums it regularly forms flowers once it reaches the surface, but they rarely open.

Because of its size, Blyxa aubertii suits only larger (especially tall) aquariums starting from 80 litres (20 gallons). Even then, it may become so large over time that it must be trimmed and divided.

This plant is definitely not for beginners. Under optimal conditions growth is moderate, and it may take a few months before it is ready for propagation.

  • Do not let the plant reach the surface, or it forms a tangled mass. Start trimming when it is 10–15 cm from the surface; it can safely be shortened by half and will grow back quickly.
  • Pull out the flower stalks: they serve no purpose and significantly weaken the plant. Removing them may turn the annual plant into a perennial one.
  • As it grows, it often becomes loose in the substrate and may need readjusting.

Planting: use it as a background plant; if it reddens it can serve as a focal point. Plant at least 20 cm apart, make sure no other plants shade it, and plant deeply enough that it does not float up. If it has few roots and keeps floating, some aquarists let it float until roots develop before planting.

Propagation: by seeds (the flowers self-pollinate) or vegetatively, which is the main method in aquariums. New shoots branch from the base; take out the plant and split it with scissors. If the new plant has no roots, leave it floating until they develop. Inspect it for decaying particles or bad leaves.

Common problems:

  • Yellow leaves or melting: low light, not enough CO2, too little (nitrogen and Fe) or too much fertilizer, unstable water parameters. It is very sensitive to Excel.
  • Root rot in alkaline water (above pH 7.0): keep parameters stable.
  • Slow growth: it prefers soft to medium water; above 5 GH it starts to float up and roots grow poorly.
  • Fragile leaves break easily during maintenance.
  • Some snails and fish eat the thin leaves.
  • It may melt after relocation or division.
  • As an annual, it needs regular propagation, otherwise it degenerates.
  • It often dies after flowering; do not let it flower.
  • It can shed leaves without apparent reason.

Temperature: 22 – 28°C. The plant does not tolerate cold water or temperature fluctuations.

pH: 5.5 – 6.8. A slightly acidic pH is more suitable; alkaline water harms the root system, so monitor pH regularly.

Hardness: it often stops growing in hard water. Ideally below 5 GH and below 3 KH.

Flow: it prefers still water; in nature it is found in stagnant or slow-flowing rivers and streams.

Lighting: moderate to high. With lower light the plant will not grow and will most probably rot. It is not for low-tech tanks. Moderate light keeps the leaves green; intense, direct light gradually turns them reddish or orange within a few days.

Substrate: in nature it is often found in clayey soil. A two-layer substrate, with a thin nutrient-rich base layer topped with fine gravel or coarse sand, is a better choice. The roots may dissolve rapidly in nutrient-rich mineral soil alone. The plant absorbs most nutrients from the water column and has a weak root system for its size.

CO2: it is extremely difficult to grow without CO2; a pressurized CO2 system is a must.

Fertilization: regular micro and macro fertilizers are necessary. Iron (0.05–0.2 mg/L) is crucial, especially under intense light, as it helps develop a reddish hue.

If you keep shrimp with this plant, note that high CO2 and copper (present in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Benefits: it is a decorative addition; it produces small pearls of oxygen on the leaves; it provides cover and shade for invertebrates, small frogs and fish; and it hosts biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.

Tankmates: best with small, peaceful community fish that will not damage it, e.g. neon tetras, clown killifish, white cloud mountain minnows, zebra danios, cherry barbs, platies, mollies, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras. For shrimp, choose species that prefer slightly acidic water, such as crystal red shrimp, blue bolt shrimp and Caridina cf. babaulti. Ornamental snails should not be kept long in low-pH water; if pH is near 7.0, almost any snail or dwarf shrimp is possible.

Avoid fish that disturb the substrate or eat the plant, e.g. silver dollars, Buenos Aires tetras, koi, goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches and African cichlids. Crayfish and freshwater crabs are also a bad combination.

Blyxa aubertii is a collective term for two varieties: var. aubertii (seeds 1.25–1.8 mm, smooth or slightly ridged, sparsely prickly, tailless) and var. echinosperma (seeds 1.5–2.0 mm without tail, ridged and prickly, with tails up to 5 mm on one or both ends). "Novoguineensis" (red version) and "Kimberley" are trade names, not recognized subspecies.

Compared with Blyxa japonica: B. japonica forms a leafy stem instead of a rosette, is smaller, is brighter green and turns only slightly reddish, and its leaves are less thin and delicate.

The genus Blyxa was established in 1806 by Francisco Noroña in Louis Marie Aubert Du Petit-Thouars' Genera Nova Madagascariensia. It belongs to the family Hydrocharitaceae, with 12 species documented.

Blyxa aubertii is a beautiful but challenging plant, suitable for experienced aquarists and not recommended for beginners.
